title: Wiping Smallpox Off the Earth
summary: In 1967, smallpox still made millions of people sick every year. A worldwide team of health workers used a tiny two-pronged needle and a clever plan: find every case, then protect everyone around it. By 1980 smallpox was gone from the whole planet, the first human disease ever wiped out.

sections.heading: A Bold Idea in Minneapolis
paragraphs: In 1958, health ministers from around the world gathered in Minneapolis, in the United States, for the yearly meeting of the World Health Assembly, the group of countries that guides the World Health Organization (WHO). One of the speakers was Viktor Zhdanov, a virus scientist who was then Deputy Minister of Health of the Soviet Union. This was the middle of the Cold War, when the Soviet Union and the United States distrusted each other and competed in almost everything, from rockets to Olympic medals. Zhdanov stood up and suggested something that sounded almost impossible: the whole world should work together to get rid of smallpox completely.

His idea was not a wild dream. Smallpox had some weaknesses that made it a good target. It only infected humans, so there were no animals where the virus could hide and come back later. People who were infected nearly always got a rash you could see, so cases were hard to miss. And there was already a vaccine that worked very well. Zhdanov also pointed out that his own country had beaten smallpox inside its borders, and he promised that the Soviet Union would donate large amounts of vaccine.

The World Health Assembly agreed, and in 1959 the global smallpox eradication programme officially began. Eradication means removing a disease from the whole world forever, not just from one country. Some countries had already managed that local step. Smallpox had stopped spreading in North America by 1952 and in Europe by 1953, thanks to vaccination, careful reporting of cases and good health services.

But the first years of the world programme went slowly. WHO had very little money for it, few staff, and many governments had other urgent problems. The main plan was mass vaccination: try to vaccinate around 80 percent of the people in every country and hope the disease would run out of people to infect. In big, crowded countries with fast-growing populations, this was like trying to empty a bathtub with a teaspoon while the tap was still running. Vaccine quality was uneven too. Some batches arriving from different makers had lost their strength in the heat before they ever reached an arm.

By the mid-1960s, smallpox was still widespread across much of Africa and South Asia, and in Brazil. In 1966, the World Health Assembly decided to try again, with a bigger budget and a fresh plan. The United States and the Soviet Union, rivals in so many ways, ended up supporting the same campaign. It was one of the rare moments in the Cold War when both sides pulled in the same direction.

sections.heading: 1967: A Fresh Start with D.A. Henderson
paragraphs: The new Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme began on 1 January 1967. To lead it, WHO chose Donald Ainslie Henderson, an American doctor usually known as D.A. Henderson. He was 38 years old, tall, energetic and famously blunt. He had been running disease surveillance programmes at the US Communicable Disease Center (now called the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC) in Atlanta, and his team there had helped plan a big smallpox and measles programme for 18 countries in western and central Africa.

Henderson moved to WHO's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland. What he faced was enormous. In 1967 smallpox was still endemic, meaning it was constantly spreading, in 31 countries. Experts estimated there were somewhere between 10 and 15 million cases a year, and about 2 million deaths. Only a small fraction of cases were ever officially reported, because many happened in remote villages far from any clinic. Part of the job was simply finding out where the disease really was.

Henderson set a target that many people thought was foolishly optimistic: smallpox should be gone in about ten years. He did not have a huge army or endless money. Instead, the programme relied on the national health services of each country, with their own vaccinators, nurses and officials, helped by a smaller group of international advisers. Over the years, staff and advisers from some 73 countries joined in. The CDC alone sent 26 young doctors and public health advisers in the early days, to help with training, transport and planning while local health workers did the vaccinating.

Henderson believed in two things above all. The first was good tools: vaccine that stayed strong in hot climates, and a simple way of giving it. The second was good information: every country needed a system for reporting each case quickly, so teams knew where to go, and every report needed checking. If a country claimed to have no smallpox, Henderson wanted to see evidence, not just hear promises.

Region by region, the map began to change. South America was cleared by 1971, with Brazil the last country there to stop the spread. Asia followed by 1975 and Africa by 1977. Each of those victories involved thousands of people, long journeys, setbacks and some very clever thinking, as you will see.

sections.heading: Two Small Tools That Changed Everything
paragraphs: The first tool was the vaccine itself. Smallpox vaccine is made from a living virus called vaccinia, a cousin of smallpox that trains the body without causing smallpox. In its old liquid form, the vaccine spoiled quickly in heat, which was a disaster in tropical countries without refrigerators. In the 1950s, British scientist Leslie Collier, working at the Lister Institute in London, improved a method for freeze-drying the vaccine. Freeze-drying means freezing a liquid and then removing the water as vapour, leaving a dry powder. Collier found that adding a protein mixture called peptone protected the virus during drying. His dried vaccine stayed effective for months even when kept at 37 degrees Celsius, about the temperature of a hot day in the tropics.

The dry powder could be carried in small glass vials for weeks across deserts and jungles. At the moment of use, the vaccinator mixed it with a little liquid. Once mixed, it only stayed good for a day or two in the heat, so teams planned carefully to use each vial quickly. During the intensified programme, WHO also checked the quality of vaccine from different factories, and donor countries, with the Soviet Union and the United States among the biggest, sent huge amounts of vaccine. Over time, more and more of it was made in laboratories inside the countries that needed it.

The second tool looked almost too simple to matter. In 1965, American microbiologist Benjamin Rubin, who worked at the drug company Wyeth, took the eye of a sewing-machine needle and ground it down to make a tiny fork with two prongs. This was the bifurcated needle, from a Latin word meaning 'two-forked'. When you dipped it into the vaccine, a single dose clung between the two prongs, held there by surface tension, the same force that lets a water droplet hang from a tap.

Using it was easy. The vaccinator held the needle upright against the upper arm and made about 15 quick jabs in a small circle about 5 millimetres across. The prongs only went into the top layer of skin, which is where the smallpox vaccine needs to be. A few days later, if the vaccine had 'taken', a small blister formed, then a scab, which fell off after two or three weeks and left a small round scar. Many grandparents still have this scar on their upper arm today.

The bifurcated needle had huge advantages. It used only about a quarter as much vaccine as older methods, so one vial could vaccinate up to about 100 people. The needles cost only about 5 US dollars per thousand, and they could be boiled or flamed and used again and again. Best of all, a person could learn to use one well in less than an hour, even with no medical training. Henderson's team adopted it for smallpox in 1967, and it was soon in use around the world. Rubin later estimated that in the final years of the campaign, about 200 million vaccinations a year were given with it. More than 7 million of these little forks were used in India alone.

sections.heading: Find the Fire, Put It Out
paragraphs: Good tools were not enough on their own. The most important change in the campaign was a new strategy, and it began with a young American doctor named William Foege, working as a medical missionary in eastern Nigeria in 1966.

When smallpox broke out in the area where he worked, Foege faced a frustrating problem: there was not nearly enough vaccine to vaccinate everybody. So instead of spreading the vaccine thinly over the whole population, he decided to aim it. Using radio messages between missionary stations and teams of local runners, he and his colleagues tracked down where the new cases were. Then they vaccinated the people around each case: family members, neighbours, and anyone who might have been in contact. They also looked for the next places the disease was likely to reach, such as villages connected by markets and family visits, and vaccinated there first.

To everyone's surprise, the outbreak stopped, even though only a fairly small share of the whole population had been vaccinated. Foege had shown that you did not need to vaccinate everyone to stop smallpox. You needed to vaccinate the right people, in the right places, quickly.

This approach became known as 'surveillance and containment'. Surveillance means watching carefully for cases and reporting them fast. Containment means building a wall of protection around each case. Later, people often called it 'ring vaccination', because you can imagine a ring of vaccinated people drawn around each sick person, and then a second ring around the contacts of those contacts. A simpler version had actually been tried in the English town of Leicester in the late 1800s, but Foege and the WHO teams turned it into a careful, organised system that could work across whole countries.

Think of smallpox like a fire jumping from house to house. Mass vaccination is like trying to soak every house in the country with water before the fire arrives. Ring vaccination is like having lookouts on hilltops who spot every new flame and then wetting all the houses around it, so the fire has nothing left to burn.

Ring vaccination worked especially well for smallpox for several reasons. People with smallpox were usually too sick to travel far, and they were most infectious once the rash appeared, so they did not usually spread it widely before anyone noticed. The rash was easy to recognise. Smallpox spread mainly through close, face-to-face contact, so the people at risk could be listed. And the vaccine could still help someone who had already been exposed, if it was given within a few days. That gave the teams a small but precious window of time.

By the late 1960s, surveillance and containment had become the heart of the whole programme. Mass vaccination did not stop completely, but the hunt for each individual case became the main job. Foege later wrote a book about these years called 'House on Fire', a title that fits his way of thinking perfectly.

sections.heading: An Army of Searchers
paragraphs: Finding every single case of a disease, in countries with hundreds of millions of people, many of them in villages without roads, telephones or electricity, was the hardest part of the job. It was done mostly by local health workers from each country, often travelling on foot, by bicycle, by boat or on the backs of animals.

The toughest fight came in South Asia. In 1974, India suffered a terrible smallpox epidemic, especially in the states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Together those two states had about three quarters of all the world's smallpox cases that year. In May 1974 alone, India recorded more than 48,000 new cases. Altogether, the epidemic infected roughly 188,000 people and about 31,000 died. Some people began to wonder if eradication was impossible after all.

Instead of giving up, India and WHO organised one of the largest health searches in history. Teams went house to house, village by village, asking the same question again and again: have you seen anyone with a rash and fever? Extra containment teams, helicopters, vaccination checkpoints on roads and railways, and hundreds of vehicles were brought in. The Tata company, which ran a large steel works in Bihar where an outbreak had spread among workers, lent doctors, vehicles and communications. Sweden gave about 14 million US dollars, and the CDC sent trained staff.

One clever tool was the smallpox recognition card. It was a small card with a clear photograph of a child with the smallpox rash. Searchers showed it to villagers, shopkeepers, teachers and schoolchildren and asked: have you seen anyone who looks like this? A picture worked even where people could not read, and it helped people tell smallpox apart from milder rashes such as chickenpox. A photograph of a child from Bangladesh became one of the most widely shown pictures in the campaign.

Another tool was the reward. Anyone who reported a real case of smallpox could receive money. As cases became rarer, the rewards grew larger, which kept people looking. Posters announced the rewards in local languages in markets, bus stations and schools. Children, who wandered everywhere and noticed everything, often turned out to be excellent reporters.

Each case that was found led to a busy routine. A guard might be posted at the house so that visitors stayed away while the patient was sick. Everyone in the house and nearby houses was vaccinated, and contacts were checked again and again for the next couple of weeks. Workers drew maps marking each case and each exposed person. The searchers came back to the same areas weeks later to make sure nothing had been missed.

The effort paid off. India's last case of smallpox was recorded in May 1975. In neighbouring Bangladesh, which had been hit hard by war, floods and the movement of refugees, teams kept searching until the very last outbreaks were found.

sections.heading: The Last Cases
paragraphs: On 16 October 1975, on her third birthday, a little girl named Rahima Banu was reported to the smallpox team. She lived in the village of Kuralia, on Bhola Island in Bangladesh, where wide rivers meet the Bay of Bengal. The person who reported her was an eight-year-old girl called Bilkisunnessa, who received a reward of 250 taka. A telegram carried the news all the way to Henderson in Geneva.

Rahima Banu had variola major, the dangerous form of smallpox. A team moved in at once. A guard stayed at her house day and night, and everyone in the village and the surrounding area was vaccinated in a ring around her. She recovered and was declared cured on 24 November 1975. No one else caught smallpox from her. She turned out to be the last person in the world to catch variola major naturally. Scabs from her illness were sent to the CDC in Atlanta, where the virus sample is still known as 'Bangladesh 1975'.

Rahima Banu grew up, married and had four children. In interviews as an adult, she has said she is proud of her small part in history, but she has also spoken honestly about how hard life has been for her family, who have lived in poverty, and about people who unfairly treated her as if she might still be dangerous. Her story reminds us that the people behind famous health milestones are real people with lives of their own.

With Asia free, the last battle moved to the Horn of Africa, first Ethiopia and then Somalia, where the milder form, variola minor, was still spreading among nomadic families who moved with their camels and goats across dry country. In 1977 teams of Somali and international workers hunted through huge distances to find each case.

On 12 October 1977, two sick children were found in a nomad camp and taken by vehicle to an isolation camp near the port town of Merca. A 23-year-old hospital cook named Ali Maow Maalin, who sometimes helped the vaccination teams, rode along to show the driver the way. The trip lasted only a few minutes, but it was enough. Maalin had never been successfully vaccinated; he later said he had been afraid of the needle.

Ten days later he became ill. At first his illness was mistaken for malaria and then chickenpox. When a nurse reported his case on 30 October and smallpox was confirmed, an enormous response began. The team found 161 people who had been in contact with him and watched them all for six weeks. Merca's hospital stopped taking new patients, checkpoints were set up around the town, and in two weeks 54,777 people were vaccinated. Nobody else caught smallpox. Maalin recovered fully.

Ali Maow Maalin was the last person in the world known to catch smallpox naturally. Years later, he turned his experience into a mission. He became a volunteer and then a local coordinator in Somalia's campaign against polio, travelling from village to village and telling hesitant parents his own story so they would understand why protecting children mattered. He died of malaria in 2013 while working on that campaign, still helping to fight the next disease.

sections.heading: One More Tragedy, Then Victory
paragraphs: There was one more, very sad chapter. In 1978, smallpox virus was still kept in a few research laboratories around the world. One of them was at the University of Birmingham Medical School in England. Janet Parker, a 40-year-old medical photographer, worked in a darkroom on the floor above the smallpox laboratory. In August 1978 she fell ill, and doctors found she had smallpox.

Health officials acted quickly. Everyone who had been near her was traced, vaccinated and watched. Her mother caught a very mild case but recovered. Sadly, Janet Parker died on 11 September 1978. She was the last known person in the world to die of smallpox.

An official inquiry led by microbiologist Reginald Shooter concluded that the virus had most likely escaped from the laboratory below, possibly carried through the air along a service duct, although exactly how she was infected has never been proven. The inquiry found that the laboratory did not meet the required safety standards. As a result, rules for working with dangerous germs in Britain became much stricter, and countries around the world decided that smallpox virus should be kept in as few places as possible.

Meanwhile, the work of proving that smallpox was really gone continued. It is very hard to prove that something no longer exists anywhere. So teams spent two years after the last natural case searching across the countries that had most recently had smallpox, following up every rumour of a rash and testing samples. Rewards were offered for reporting any case at all. Every rumour turned out to be something else, such as chickenpox or measles.

In December 1979, an independent Global Commission of scientists from many countries, meeting at WHO headquarters in Geneva, signed a statement certifying that smallpox had been eradicated. Then, on 8 May 1980, the 33rd World Health Assembly officially declared that the world and all its peoples had won freedom from smallpox. It was almost two centuries since Edward Jenner had vaccinated James Phipps in 1796.

Smallpox was the first human disease ever eradicated, and it is still the only one. Because the disease was gone, the World Health Assembly recommended that countries could stop routine smallpox vaccination, and over the following years they did. Many children born after the 1970s have never needed a smallpox vaccine, which is why younger people usually do not have the little round scar their grandparents may have. The only other disease humans have ever eradicated is rinderpest, a deadly illness of cattle and buffalo. Its last confirmed case was in Kenya in 2001, and its eradication was confirmed in 2011.

sections.heading: Two Locked Freezers and a Big Debate
paragraphs: After the Birmingham tragedy, laboratories around the world destroyed their smallpox samples or sent them to safer places. In 1981 four countries still held the virus. By 1984 only two official stores were left, and that is still true today: one at the CDC in Atlanta, in the United States, and one at the VECTOR research centre in Koltsovo, in Russia. Both are high-security laboratories built for the most dangerous germs, and WHO inspects them regularly.

Ever since, people have argued about whether these last samples should be destroyed. Those who want them destroyed say that as long as the virus exists, there is a small risk it could escape or be misused, and that keeping it goes against the whole point of eradication. In 1996, the World Health Assembly agreed that the stocks should be destroyed in June 1999.

But others argued that scientists still needed the live virus to develop better tests, safer vaccines and medicines, just in case smallpox ever came back, for example from a secret or forgotten sample. In 2002, the World Health Assembly allowed the samples to be kept for a while longer, only for approved research. An expert committee meets every year to check what research is being done and whether it is still needed.

The worry about forgotten samples is not just imagination. In 2014, workers clearing out an old storeroom at a US government laboratory in Bethesda, Maryland, found six sealed glass vials labelled 'variola' from the 1950s. Tests showed that virus in at least two of them could still grow. They were destroyed under WHO observation in 2015. The discovery showed how carefully old laboratories need to be checked.

Today the debate continues, with sensible people on both sides. Meanwhile, the legacy of the eradication programme lives on in other ways. The surveillance and containment ideas it pioneered have been used against other diseases, including ring vaccination against Ebola in the 2010s. Many of the people trained in the smallpox campaign went on to lead health programmes around the world, and its success gave energy to new efforts, including the campaigns against polio and Guinea worm disease.

The smallpox story proved something people had not been sure of before: that countries which disagreed about almost everything could work together to defeat a disease everywhere, forever. And while the hunt for the last cases of smallpox was going on, scientists in other laboratories were busy creating a whole new set of vaccines to protect children from measles, mumps, rubella and many other diseases.

deepDive: Why could smallpox be eradicated when so many other diseases cannot? Epidemiologists usually point to a combination of biological and practical features. Variola virus had no animal reservoir, so once human-to-human transmission stopped, there was nowhere for it to survive in nature. There was no long-term carrier state: people either recovered with lasting immunity or died, and nobody silently carried the virus for years. Infection almost always produced an obvious, distinctive rash, so cases could be found by non-specialists using a picture card. Transmission mostly needed close, prolonged contact, and patients were most infectious after the rash appeared, which limited spread before detection. Finally, a single dose of vaccinia vaccine gave strong protection, and vaccination within a few days after exposure could still prevent or soften disease. Compare this with polio, where most infections cause no symptoms at all, so each visible case of paralysis hides many silent infections, or measles, which is far more contagious and spreads before the rash appears. Historians also debate how much credit belongs to strategy versus resources. The shift from mass vaccination toward surveillance and containment is often presented as the key insight, but in practice the two worked together: high background vaccination levels slowed spread so that containment teams could keep up, and in dense areas like Bihar both approaches ran side by side. Another debate concerns cost-effectiveness. The intensified programme cost a few hundred million US dollars over about a decade, including spending by the affected countries themselves, while the savings from no longer vaccinating, treating cases or checking travellers' vaccination certificates are generally estimated to have repaid that investment many times over every year. Historians such as those writing about the Cold War also stress the politics: a Soviet proposal, American leadership, and money from both superpowers made it a rare cooperative project. Finally, the decision to keep the last variola stocks remains unresolved, balancing the small risk of keeping live virus against the research value of having it to test new antiviral medicines and diagnostic tools.
funFact: The bifurcated needle that helped wipe out smallpox was made by grinding down the eye of an ordinary sewing-machine needle, and the needles cost only about 5 US dollars per thousand.
